stages.act: Notices a new order on a worklist, or is handed a printout.
stages.pain: There is no reliable signal that an order needs authorisation. It is knowledge held in a person's head, a spreadsheet, or a payer PDF from last year.
stages.after: The case already exists. It was opened by the Intake Agent the moment the physician selected the order, with the payer's own answer attached.

stages.act: Logs into a payer portal, or calls, to confirm coverage and whether authorisation is needed.
stages.pain: A different portal and a different password for each payer. Hold music. Answers that are not written down anywhere afterwards.
stages.after: Coverage, benefit tier, member cost share and the document list arrive from CRD in seconds, and are attached to the case as evidence.

stages.act: Hunts through the EHR, calls the PT clinic, requests outside records by fax.
stages.pain: The single largest time sink. Records sit in systems the coordinator has no login for, and there is no way to know what is missing until the payer says so.
stages.after: The Clinical Evidence Agent queries every connected source at once and returns a ranked evidence set — plus an explicit list of what it could not find.

stages.act: Retypes clinical facts into a payer questionnaire, per payer, per patient.
stages.touch: Payer portal form · PDF · fax cover sheet
stages.pain: Every field is data that already exists somewhere in the chart. Transcription is slow and introduces errors that cause pends.
stages.after: DTR renders the payer's own questionnaire and the platform autofills it. The coordinator answers only what the plan genuinely does not know.

stages.act: Checks the packet, submits, writes down a reference number.
stages.pain: Submitting is the easy part. Knowing whether the packet was strong enough is guesswork until a decision arrives days later.
stages.after: The review screen shows each criterion, the evidence behind it, and a confidence score. The coordinator approves with their name on it — this step stays human.

stages.act: Calls or checks portals repeatedly; handles requests for more information.
stages.pain: Days of polling. A request for more information can sit unnoticed and quietly blow the SLA.
stages.after: Status arrives by push. A pend reason becomes a named evidence task, and a new result landing in the repository can satisfy it automatically.

name: Ordering physician
who: Specialist or primary care, in clinic
tag: Wants to place the order and move on

stages.act: Determines the study or drug is indicated.
stages.pain: No idea whether this patient's plan covers it, needs authorisation, or prefers a different agent. That information arrives days later, via staff.
stages.after: A CDS card appears while the order is still being written: covered, authorisation required, here is what will be needed — and sometimes, here is a covered alternative.

stages.pain: The order is signed into a void. The authorisation process is invisible to the physician from here on.
stages.after: Signing the order is what starts the case. The physician sees it start, and can see its state later without asking anyone.

stages.act: Responds to staff messages asking for documentation, sometimes weeks later.
stages.pain: Context-switching back into a patient they saw three weeks ago, to restate something already written in a note.
stages.after: Autofill removes most of it. What remains is two or three genuinely clinical questions, asked once, inside the chart, while context is still fresh.

stages.act: Schedules and takes a call with a payer medical director.
stages.pain: Preparation means re-reading the whole chart. Often the call is about a document that existed all along and simply was not sent.
stages.after: The Denial & Appeal Agent produces a briefing sheet: the criterion cited, the evidence that answers it, and what has changed since submission.

stages.act: Has to say they do not know.
stages.pain: Erodes trust, and the physician genuinely has no visibility.
stages.after: Status is visible in the chart, and the patient has already been told directly.

name: Patient
tag: Usually the last to be told anything

stages.act: Told the office will 'get it approved'.
stages.pain: No timeline, no idea what authorisation even is, no idea what it will cost.
stages.after: A message before they reach the car: the request has been opened, here is the expected decision date, here is your estimated share of cost.

stages.pain: Silence. The most common complaint in the whole process, and the one that generates the most inbound calls.
stages.after: Status updates at each transition, in plain language, on the channel they consented to.

stages.act: Lives with the untreated problem while the paperwork moves.
stages.pain: The clinical cost of delay is real and is borne entirely by the patient.
stages.after: Turnaround measured in hours rather than weeks is the outcome that actually matters here. Everything else is operational.

stages.act: Told by the office that the plan said no.
stages.pain: Frightening, and usually unexplained. Most patients do not know an appeal is possible.
stages.after: Told what was denied, on what specific ground, what happens next, and that an appeal has already been drafted for their physician to review.

stages.act: Books the study or starts the drug.
stages.pain: Often a second delay: the authorisation exists but scheduling did not know.
stages.after: The authorisation is written back to the order, so scheduling opens the moment the decision lands.
